newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Germany shifts market focus.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Germany shifts market focus.

text.p: Gold dealers face a whole new focus this week following news of Germany's plan to revalue its reserves closer to market figures, traders and analysts said.
The shock was compounded by gold being linked to Germany's 1997 budget problems and, in the longer term, to the country's ability to steer through European Monetary Union entrance criteria.
Revaluing Germany's near 3,000 tonne gold hoard would give its finances an on-paper windfall of around 40 billion marks, economists estimate.
"Gold's innocence has been lost. Now it will have to perform as any other (reserve) asset," said bullion market analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland.

That automatically increased the risk of the reserves being sold if they did not make a profit, gold dealers were quick to emphasises -- despite Germany's Finance Minister Theo Waigel stating none would be sold. Germany has never been even a lender of gold to the market.
"It means the risk premium may be too high. Somebody looking at gold versus other investments with all this hanging about it is more likely to say, 'Why bother?'" Smith added.

Gold closed last Friday at $344.50/$345.00 per ounce, its lowest close during a week in which it had appeared to established itself at slightly higher levels between $346.00 and $351.00. It was $1.25 lower on Monday
"As soon as it seems safe to go back in (to gold), up pops another central bank," said Rhona O'Connell, metal markets analyst at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co.
Helping gold rally last week and cushioning the fall of barely a couple of dollars on the Bundesbank news was a weakening dollar, esepcially against the yen.
"The yen is being seen as a measure of how much the dollar was overvalued and it is telling us it is overvalued," one senior dealer said.
"That must mean the Dow (Jones Industrial Average) is probably overvalued too," the dealer said, adding that longer term he did not see this being bullish for gold.
As well as grappling with a new and bearish background, technically gold could be in for a testing week, analysts said.

"The charts were showing a bullish flag pattern (last week) but that has gone a bit pear-shaped now," one analyst said, referring to gold's inability to break out past the $351.00 resistance that had capped it early last week.

Silver added to gold's woes last Friday. After reaching its highest price since April midweek, it slipped to become friendless on Thursday before the investment funds unloaded it on Friday, inducing an intra-day fall of 15 cents to $4.70/$4.71. It was a cent lower on Monday morning
"Silver is very risky just now.I would not be surprised to see it 20 cents lower still," one dealer said.
Platinum and palladium were both a little lower at the end of last week, having caught the wash off silver's dive.
But prices have stayed high even though Russia appears to be on the verge of sitting down with the Japanese trading houses to discuss 1997 export contracts for the first time this year.
Lending rates of over 25 percent for one month were quoted last week reflecting the extreme shortage of metal in the market resulting from the Russian export delays.
Russia is the largest exporter of palladium and second largest supplier of platinum while Japanese is the biggest importer of both metals.
Platinum closed on Friday at $390.75/$391.75 and was a couple of dollars lower on Monday. Palladium was at $170.00/$171.00 on Friday, and showed little change early Monday.
--Brian Spoors London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
